RAG systems are evaluated on several dimensions including faithfulness (whether the answer is supported by the retrieved context), answer relevancy (whether the answer addresses the question), context precision (whether retrieved chunks are relevant), and context recall (whether all necessary information was retrieved). Hybrid retrieval combines dense vector search with sparse keyword-based methods such as BM25. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is a common technique for merging results from multiple retrieval methods into a single ranked list. Reranking is an optional step that uses a cross-encoder model to re-score candidate chunks based on their relevance to the query. Cross-encoders are more accurate than bi-encoders for relevance scoring but are slower because they process query and document together rather than independently. Chunking strategy significantly affects retrieval quality. Fixed-size chunking splits documents into equal-length windows, while semantic chunking uses sentence embeddings to identify natural topic boundaries. Semantic chunking tends to produce more coherent and self-contained chunks, which improves both retrieval precision and generation faithfulness. Hallucination is a key failure mode in LLM-based systems, where the model generates plausible-sounding but factually incorrect statements not grounded in the provided context. Strict system prompts and citation requirements are common mitigations used to reduce hallucination rates in RAG systems. The RAGAS framework provides standardized metrics for evaluating RAG pipelines: Faithfulness, Answer Relevancy, Context Precision, Context Recall, and Answer Correctness. These metrics enable systematic comparison across different configurations of chunking strategy, retrieval method, and generation model.
